summary: This clipped Digital Leadership web article explains the cost structure building block of the Business Model Canvas and why it matters for profitability and innovation. It defines cost structure as all the ways a business pays its bills, gives examples of fixed, variable, operating, customer acquisition, distribution and after-sales costs, and begins discussing cost structure types such as fixed cost structure. The note is cut off mid-article, and much of its text is site navigation and promotional material that was ignored.
one_line: Digital Leadership article defining the Cost Structure building block of the Business Model Canvas, with cost examples and cost structure types.
key_facts: Cost Structure refers to all the ways a business approaches paying its bills, such as the fixed cost of building rental, the variable cost of hourly wages, and the sometimes-unpredictable costs of repairs or disaster response.
Cost Structure is the aggregate of all the ways a business must spend money, and companies can use it within an overall Business Model to identify where expenses can be reduced.
Cost structures play a key role in the Cost Model of the Business Model Canvas and help guide how a business targets innovation and value proposition development.
Cost Structure is one of the building blocks of the Business Model Canvas, which was designed by Digital Leadership AG building on the work of Alexander Osterwalder.
Fixed Costs are costs that remain relatively constant regardless of the level of production or sales, such as rent or lease payments, salaries and benefits, insurance, depreciation and utilities.
Variable Costs fluctuate based on the level of production or sales and include raw materials, manufacturing costs, sales commissions, shipping and freight, and Cost of Goods Sold (COGS).

Operating Costs are ongoing expenses essential for running day-to-day operations, including marketing and advertising, research and development (R&D), IT infrastructure, customer support and office supplies.
Customer Acquisition Costs (CAC) are the cost incurred to acquire a new customer, including marketing campaigns, sales team expenses, and free trials or discounts.
Distribution Costs cover delivering products or services to customers, such as warehousing and costs of third-party distributors or sales channels.
After-Sales Support costs include warranty and repairs for defective products and customer service for post-sale inquiries or issues.
The article states that Cost Structures need to be intentional, and that unless a business has made a selection and followed through, it is probably experiencing unnecessary costs.

The Fixed Cost structure section states that the most predictable kinds of costs are Fixed Costs, and that these costs are incurred no matter how many goods or services the business produces, such as rent, insurance, or loan payments.
The article was published on 19 July, 2023 and written by Stefan F. Dieffenbacher, listed as Founder, with an estimated reading time of 22 minutes.
The Key Activities building block notes that key activities should never be outsourced, while tangential activities such as copy machine maintenance can be handled by contractors.
